opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a very interesting argument, and historically an important one, but I'd say it rests on an assumption about how much information is really in the data and how efficiently a learner can extract it. The argument says, roughly, that children hear a limited, noisy set of sentences, yet they generalize to infinitely many new grammatical sentences, so there must be strong innate structure. That intuition is reasonable, but it was formulated before we had any quantitative way to ask: how many examples do you actually need to learn a hierarchical, compositional structure?

That's what we've been trying to address with simple models. For instance, we study synthetic data generated by a random hierarchical grammar, a sort of tree of production rules, where meaning is built compositionally from parts. What you find is that if the learner is naive, something like a kernel method or anything that treats the input as an unstructured high-dimensional object, the number of examples you need explodes. That's the curse of dimensionality, and in that regime the poverty-of-stimulus argument would look very convincing.

But deep networks behave differently. They can exploit correlations between low-level tokens and the higher-level latent variables, essentially discovering synonyms and building up the hierarchy level by level. And then the number of samples needed scales only polynomially, not exponentially. Even more interesting, you see a kind of stepwise learning: as the training set grows, the network can resolve correlations at larger and larger distances, and it learns deeper levels of the structure. So the "creativity," the ability to produce or recognize sentences never seen, emerges from learning the compositional rules rather than memorizing examples.

So my assessment would be: the argument is correct that a learner without the right inductive bias can't do it. But the needed bias may be much more generic than a language-specific universal grammar. It may be enough to have an architecture that is local, hierarchical, and able to build representations invariant to irrelevant variations. Whether the brain has exactly that, and whether real language statistics are rich enough in the way our models assume, are open empirical questions. But I don't think one can anymore say, as a matter of principle, that learning from examples cannot explain linguistic creativity. The question has become quantitative, and that's progress.

r001.rationale: It describes creativity as producing or recognizing sentences never seen before, and frames the target as new grammatical sentences built from compositional rules.

r002.rationale: It does not say that the same finite examples can be fit by both a context-free grammar and a regular grammar.

r003.rationale: It says naive or kernel learners need many examples, but does not state that shallow networks fail in the hierarchical model.

r004.rationale: It says deep networks exploit token correlations and build the hierarchy level by level, describing hierarchical representations learned by deep architectures.

r005.rationale: It says sample needs scale polynomially, but does not specify that the polynomial is in sentence length.

r006.rationale: It proposes a generic local, hierarchical architecture as a source of bias, but does not say that this architecture is innate.

r007.rationale: It questions whether language-specific universal grammar is needed, but does not clearly distinguish challenging the poverty-of-stimulus argument from disproving innate linguistic structure.

fable-5.1.text:
So, I think it's a fascinating question, and I come at it from the point of view of physics, so I'll try to be careful. The poverty-of-stimulus argument says, roughly, children hear a finite, actually fairly small and noisy set of sentences, and yet they generalize to an essentially infinite set of grammatical sentences, and they almost never produce certain kinds of errors that you would expect if they were just doing some naive statistics. So the conclusion is that there must be a strong prior, an innate structure, a universal grammar.

Now, I think the empirical observation is interesting, but the inference is where I'm skeptical, because it rests on an intuition about what "learning from examples" can do, and that intuition was formed before we had systems that actually learn from examples at scale. If you look at what we have learned about neural networks in the last ten years, the lesson is really that the question "how many examples do you need" is not answered by counting hypotheses or by some generic argument about the size of the space. It is answered by the structure of the data and by the inductive bias of the learning architecture, and these two things together can make the sample complexity enormously smaller than the naive estimate.

What we have been trying to do in my group is to make this quantitative. If you consider data that have a hierarchical, compositional structure, something like a generative grammar, where high-level features are made of combinations of lower-level features, and so on, you can ask how many examples a deep network needs to learn the task. And what you find is that the sample complexity grows polynomially with the size of the input, rather than exponentially, as it would for a method that is not able to exploit the structure. The reason, essentially, is that the network learns the low-level building blocks first, because they are the ones where the correlation with the label is easiest to detect, and then it builds up from there, level by level. So the depth of the architecture matches the depth of the grammar, and that is the inductive bias that does the work.

So in that sense, I would say the poverty-of-stimulus argument is partly right and partly wrong. It is right that a prior is needed. Any learning that generalizes needs a bias, this is just a mathematical fact. But the prior that is needed may be much weaker and much more generic than a universal grammar of a specific linguistic form. Something like "the world is compositional and hierarchical, and I am a hierarchical machine that learns the simplest correlations first" may be sufficient to get you very far. And of course, language models are a kind of existence proof here. They are not trained on anything like the data a child sees, so one should not over-interpret, but they clearly show that linguistic creativity, in the sense of producing new, grammatical, meaningful sentences, is not out of reach of learning from examples.

Where I think the honest answer is that we don't know is on the quantitative side. A child sees maybe tens of millions of words, a large model sees a trillion. That gap is real, and it is the kind of thing that should be explained rather than argued away. It may be that the brain has stronger priors, it may be that interaction with the world, grounding, provides much richer signal per example than text, it may be that we are still far from the right architecture. But I think these are now experimental questions about sample complexity, and that is the right place for the debate to be, rather than in a priori claims about what statistics can or cannot do.

r001.rationale: It describes linguistic creativity as producing new grammatical sentences, which conveys previously unheard sentences that obey syntactic constraints.

r002.rationale: It does not say that the same finite sentence set can be fit by both a context-free and a regular grammar.

r003.rationale: It does not state that shallow networks fail in Wyart’s idealized hierarchical model.

r004.rationale: It says a deep network’s depth can match the grammar’s hierarchy and explains that it learns building blocks level by level.

r005.rationale: It states that sample complexity grows polynomially with input size for hierarchical, compositional data, rather than exponentially.

r006.rationale: It suggests a hierarchical machine and generic compositional prior, but does not propose that an innate deep architecture supplies much of the needed bias.

r007.rationale: It questions the inference to universal grammar but does not distinguish refuting the poverty-of-stimulus argument from proving innate linguistic structure false.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to distinguish two claims. One is that learning requires some inductive bias. Of course it does: you never infer a rule from examples without some assumptions about what kinds of rules are plausible. But the stronger claim—that learning from examples cannot produce linguistic creativity—seems much harder to defend.

Learning is not necessarily memorizing sentences. You can learn regularities that allow you to construct sentences you have never encountered. So the fact that a child produces a new sentence does not, by itself, tell us that the relevant grammatical structure had to be specified in advance.

Language models make that distinction particularly interesting. They suggest that learning from examples can produce quite rich linguistic generalization. But they see much more text than a child, so that is not a complete explanation of human language acquisition. The sharper question is: what biases allow children to learn so efficiently from the information available to them? That is a quantitative question about learning, rather than an argument that learning cannot explain creativity.

r001.rationale: It says learning can construct sentences never encountered, but does not define creativity as producing sentences that obey syntactic constraints.

r002.rationale: It does not compare context-free and regular grammars fitting the same finite examples.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss shallow networks or Wyart’s idealized hierarchical generative model.

r004.rationale: It does not say deep architectures implicitly favor hierarchical representations.

r005.rationale: It gives no polynomial sample-size claim or sentence-length relationship for Wyart’s model.

r006.rationale: It asks what biases enable efficient learning, but does not propose an innate deep architecture as the source of that bias.

r007.rationale: It questions whether examples alone explain creativity, but does not clearly distinguish refuting the poverty-of-stimulus argument from disproving innate linguistic structure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there is a real question there, but I don’t think the conclusion follows. Children learn from a finite number of examples, and then they can produce sentences they have never heard. But that is precisely what we mean by generalization. A learning system need not memorize sentences; it can discover structure that allows it to combine things in new ways.

Of course, learning requires some inductive bias. The interesting question is how much of that bias must be specific to language, and how much can come from more general mechanisms. The success of language models makes it harder to argue that learning from examples is fundamentally incapable of producing this kind of creativity. But those models typically see far more text than a child, so they don’t settle the question of how children learn so efficiently.

For me, the productive approach is to make the argument quantitative: what structure can be learned, from how many examples, and with which assumptions? Novel sentences alone don’t establish that the underlying rules must be innate.

r001.rationale: It describes producing unheard sentences through generalization, but does not say those sentences obey syntactic constraints.

r002.rationale: It does not compare context-free and regular grammars fitting the same examples.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim about shallow networks or Wyart’s idealized model.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss deep architectures or their preference for hierarchical representations.

r005.rationale: It gives no sample-size result involving a number of sentences polynomial in sentence length.

r006.rationale: It discusses inductive bias generally, but does not propose an innate deep architecture as its source.

r007.rationale: It says language models make it harder to argue that learning from examples cannot produce creativity, while noting they do not settle how children learn efficiently; it also says novel sentences alone do not establish that rules must be innate.
